stages.title: Pluggable optical modules (today)
stages.summary: Today most switch optics live in removable modules on the front of the box (faceplate). They convert electricity to light and back. Easy to swap, but they burn power and take space — which gets painful as AI fabrics push higher bandwidth.

stages.title: Co-packaged optics (CPO) package
stages.summary: Instead of optics at the faceplate, the optical engines sit next to the switch chip on the same package. Shorter electrical traces mean less power and higher bandwidth for linking AI racks (scale-out).

stages.title: End state — CPO default for AI scale-out
stages.summary: Industry maps expect co-packaged optics to become the normal way AI scale-out switches connect racks at the highest bandwidths — not a niche demo. Timing is a ramp across the late 2020s, not a single overnight flip.

stages.title: Switch ASIC
stages.summary: The networking brain: an Ethernet or InfiniBand chip that decides where packets go between racks. In a CPO design it still sits at the center; optics move closer to it instead of living only in front-panel modules.

stages.title: Photonic engine (TSMC COUPE-class)
stages.summary: A photonic engine turns electrical signals from the switch into light (and back). TSMC’s Compact Universal Photonic Engine (COUPE) is a foundry recipe for putting that engine beside high-speed chips.

stages.title: External light source (ELS) fiber feed
stages.summary: Lasers often live off the hot switch package. Fiber brings their light into the photonic engines. That lets operators cool, share, and eventually swap lasers without tearing apart the switch package.

stages.title: Optical ports
stages.summary: The fibers leaving the switch toward other racks. AI scale-out designs aim at very high lane rates (for example 800 gigabits per second class) so whole clusters can talk without copper walls.

stages.title: NVIDIA Quantum-X Photonics
stages.summary: NVIDIA’s InfiniBand co-packaged optics platform for AI clusters — about 144 ports at 800 gigabits per second class. Aimed at scale-out fabrics where racks must exchange huge volumes of training and inference traffic.

Platform discussions include assemblers such as Delta / Micas and validation paths with buyers such as Meta.

stages.title: Becoming mainstream (2026–2028)
stages.summary: The window when co-packaged optics moves from flagship announcements into normal planning for new AI scale-out networks — still early volume, but no longer science-fair only.

stages.title: Volume wave (2027–2028)
stages.summary: The shipment ramp many industry maps mark as the first real volume wave for AI scale-out CPO — when more vendors and buyers move from trials to production orders.

stages.title: Still ramping through 2030
stages.summary: Adoption does not stop after the first wave. Newer halls and refreshes continue taking CPO as copper and pluggable options strain at the highest AI bandwidths.

stages.title: GPU / accelerator die
stages.summary: The chip that trains and runs models. Scale-up optical I/O is about linking many of these dies (or packages) tightly — today often with copper meshes; tomorrow more often with light on the package.

stages.title: Serializer/deserializer (SerDes)
stages.summary: High-speed electrical I/O that turns parallel chip data into fast serial streams (and back). In the optical scale-up endgame, SerDes drives a modulator instead of a long copper cable for that hop.

companies.name: Broadcom
companies.note: SerDes IP in many networking chips

stages.title: Optical modulator
stages.summary: A tiny device that imprints electrical bits onto a beam of light (bright/dim or phase shifts). It is how a GPU package “talks” optically without putting a whole pluggable module on every link.

stages.title: Photodetector
stages.summary: Turns incoming light back into electricity so the receiving GPU can read the bits. Paired with the modulator on the other end of the fiber.

stages.title: Fiber to peer GPU
stages.summary: Glass fiber carries the light between GPU packages. For scale-up domains this can replace thick copper cable bundles once rates and distances make copper painful.

stages.title: External light source for scale-up
stages.summary: The laser does not have to sit on every hot GPU package. An external light source feeds multiple optical engines, which helps cooling, serviceability, and sharing expensive laser capacity.

stages.title: End state — optical scale-up hop
stages.summary: GPU SerDes drives the modulator; an external laser feeds light; detectors recover bits at the peer. No separate switch ASIC is needed for that particular GPU-to-GPU hop (scale-out switches still matter between racks).

companies.name: NVIDIA
companies.note: Defines when copper vs optical wins inside its scale-up domains

stages.title: Ayar Labs (TeraPHY + SuperNova)
stages.summary: Private company building optical I/O chiplets (TeraPHY) and multi-wavelength light sources (SuperNova). Frequently shown at Optical Fiber Communication Conference (OFC) and Hot Chips-style venues.

stages.title: Lightmatter Passage
stages.summary: Private company working on optical interconnect approaches (Passage) aimed at moving bits with light between accelerators and packages.

stages.title: Vendor-optimistic volume window
stages.summary: Suppliers often pitch volume earlier (roughly 2027–2029). Treat as marketing-tilted timing until independent and buyer roadmaps agree.

stages.title: Analyst-style volume timing
stages.summary: Independent framing (for example SemiAnalysis-style notes) often keeps copper through much of near-term NVIDIA scale-up generations, with meaningful optical scale-up volume later — late 2028 into 2029 in some maps.

stages.title: TSMC foundry role (COUPE)
stages.summary: Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company offers Compact Universal Photonic Engine (COUPE): a path to build silicon-photonics engines and package them beside advanced compute or switch dies.

stages.title: Platform customers
stages.summary: Chip and system vendors that adopt COUPE-class engines so their switches or accelerators can ship with optics beside the die instead of only as pluggable modules.

stages.title: End state — COUPE as a building block
stages.summary: Optics beside compute or switch dies at manufacturing scale — COUPE treated like other advanced-packaging bricks buyers can design around.

stages.title: 2026 substrate-level CPO
stages.summary: Early COUPE generation aimed at substrate-level co-packaged optics with about 200 gigabits per second per lane using microring modulators.

stages.title: ~2027 — 6.4 terabits per second class
stages.summary: Next bandwidth step on the published COUPE path — more total throughput through the photonic engine as AI fabrics demand it.

stages.title: 12.8 Tb/s on-interposer (pathfinding)
stages.summary: Putting still-faster optics on the interposer (the wiring layer inside the package). Marked as pathfinding — interesting engineering, not a promised ship date.

stages.title: By 2030 — edge density goal
stages.summary: Aim for roughly 4 terabits per second per millimeter of package edge — packing more optical bandwidth into the same physical outline beside compute.

stages.title: Microring modulators
stages.summary: Tiny ring-shaped devices on a silicon chip that imprint data onto light. They are a core building block in many silicon-photonics engines, including COUPE-class designs.

stages.title: On-interposer optics
stages.summary: An interposer is a fine wiring layer inside a chip package. Putting optics there means light engines share the same package neighborhood as compute dies — shorter electrical hops.

stages.title: Edge density goal
stages.summary: How much optical bandwidth you can squeeze along each millimeter of the package edge. Higher density lets AI systems grow bandwidth without ballooning package size.

stages.title: ELS / ELSFP architecture
stages.summary: External light source (sometimes discussed as ELSFP-class modules) keeps lasers off the hottest packages. Roughly 30% wall-plug efficiency class is a common orientation figure for these laser systems — energy in versus light out.

stages.title: Why keep lasers external?
stages.summary: Lasers dislike heat, fail as field-replaceable parts, and are expensive to duplicate on every engine. Off-package sources can be cooled properly, shared across engines, and swapped when they age.

stages.title: End state — swappable multi-wavelength ELS
stages.summary: Data-center optical engines are fed by shared, swappable multi-wavelength external light sources — hot lasers are not glued onto every co-packaged engine.

stages.title: Lumentum
stages.summary: Public photonics company supplying lasers and optical engines, including capacity often discussed for AI co-packaged optics and external light sources.

stages.title: Coherent
stages.summary: Public photonics company with lasers and a broad optics portfolio spanning communications and industrial uses — another named supplier in AI optics laser narratives.

stages.title: NVIDIA–laser capacity ties
stages.summary: Industry coverage ties NVIDIA’s AI optics ramps to laser capacity from suppliers such as Lumentum and Coherent around the 2026 window — lasers become a shared bottleneck story with CPO.

stages.title: Ayar SuperNova
stages.summary: Ayar Labs’ multi-wavelength external light source: many colors (channels) of light from one module so one fiber can carry many data streams (wavelength-division multiplexing). Private company.

stages.title: Multi-wavelength (WDM) light
stages.summary: Wavelength-division multiplexing sends several independent channels as different colors of light in one fiber — multiplying bandwidth without multiplying fiber count.

stages.title: Upstream indium phosphide wafers
stages.summary: Many communications lasers grow on compound-semiconductor wafers such as indium phosphide (InP). Substrate makers sit upstream of laser chip factories.

stages.title: Universal Chiplet Interconnect Express (UCIe)
stages.summary: An industry standard for short, fast electrical links between chiplets inside a package. For optical I/O, UCIe-class bridges connect a compute die to an optical chiplet sitting beside it.

stages.title: Laser multi-source agreement (MSA)
stages.summary: A multi-source agreement lets several vendors build compatible modules — common plugs, sizes, and behaviors — so buyers are not locked to one laser supplier’s proprietary shape.

stages.title: Optical protocols (less settled)
stages.summary: Copper serializer/deserializer (SerDes) links have mature, widely understood protocols. Optical chiplet and CPO protocols are still catching up — more vendor-specific choices remain.

stages.title: Copper SerDes as the maturity reference
stages.summary: Engineers compare optical options to copper SerDes: cost, power, reach, and how interchangeable parts are across vendors. Copper is the “settled” baseline optical must match for mix-and-match comfort.

stages.title: Cross-vendor interoperability
stages.summary: The goal: mix engines, lasers, and chiplets from different suppliers the way buyers already mix copper cables and pluggables — without a full custom redesign each time.

companies.note: Foundry packaging that multiple customers share

stages.title: End state — settled optical I/O standards
stages.summary: UCIe-class die bridges, laser multi-source agreements, and optical protocols become as interchangeable in practice as copper SerDes links — lowering lock-in and speeding adoption.

stages.title: Optical chiplet
stages.summary: A small die dedicated to photonic I/O that sits beside a compute or switch die in the same package — connected electrically over a short chiplet link, optically over fiber.

stages.title: Electrical bridge on package
stages.summary: The short UCIe-class (or similar) electrical hop between a compute die and an optical chiplet. It replaces long board traces that would otherwise fight high lane rates.

companies.name: Ayar Labs
companies.note: Needs a die-to-die bridge to the host (private)

stages.title: Ecosystem bodies
stages.summary: Consortia and multi-source agreement groups write the paperwork that lets vendors claim compatibility. Slow, but how copper and pluggable optics became interchangeable.
